documents.unit: University Center for Teaching and Learning
documents.title: The Prompt: Teaching with Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page says "Decide what role, if any, AI should play" and puts the choice with each instructor, and sets no university rule. The saved text lists no tiers, so tiers is empty.
documents.summary: A teaching-center guide hub with links on reflecting on values, developing, implementing and enforcing a course AI policy, and using AI in teaching. The saved page is a landing page with tile blurbs, so the templates named in the collect notes are not in the text.

units.why: The page opens its policy section with a usage statistic: "Nearly 90% of all U.S. college students use AI for their academic work." It is a fact offered as the reason course AI policies need attention, so it is informs, and no type covers a usage statistic used as justification.
units.anchor: Nearly 90% of all U.S. college students use AI for their academic work.
units.uncovered_note: States a statistic on student AI use as the reason instructors must attend to AI in teaching and course design.

units.why: "Decide what role, if any, AI should play" tells each instructor to settle their own course's AI role, so the decision sits with the instructor (P04); it is not a tier list (P05).
units.anchor: Decide what role, if any, AI should play

units.why: "Communicate your values and expectations" asks instructors to make their course AI rules explicit; P09 is the nearest type, but the text names no syllabus and says values as well as rules.
units.anchor: Communicate your values and expectations.
units.fit_note: Does not name the syllabus; asks instructors to communicate their values as well as the rules.

units.why: "Respond appropriately if questions arise" is brief advice on enforcing a course AI policy. P123 (say how misuse will be handled) is nearest but the text gives no detail.
units.anchor: Respond appropriately if questions arise.
units.fit_note: Only says to respond appropriately when questions about AI use arise; no detection or handling method is stated.

units.why: "Surfacing and examining your values and assumptions with careful reflection helps you to be intentional" asks instructors to weigh their own values before choosing AI commitments; P118 (weigh benefits, risks and values) fits, though it is addressed to instructors rather than users in general.
units.anchor: Surfacing and examining your values and assumptions with careful reflection
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors choosing course commitments, not to users deciding whether to use AI.

units.why: "AI hasn't changed the fundamentals of effective teaching" frames AI as a reason to apply learning science, an assignment-design principle rather than a rule. No type covers a claim that teaching fundamentals are unchanged by AI.
units.anchor: AI hasn’t changed the fundamentals of effective teaching.
units.frag_end: apply the science of learning thoughtfully.
units.uncovered_note: Claims AI does not change the fundamentals of effective teaching and gives new reasons to apply the science of learning.

units.why: "Create learning experiences that encourage students to invest in their own learning" is assignment-design advice offered in an AI context; P35 is nearest but no AI-specific redesign is described.
units.anchor: Create learning experiences that encourage students to invest in their own learning.
units.fit_note: General assignment-design principle; does not describe an AI-specific redesign.

units.why: "Help students understand AI's capabilities and limitations in your discipline" makes AI a course topic, so courses teach about AI; P44 is nearest, though the text stresses limitations as well as skills.
units.anchor: Help students understand AI’s capabilities and limitations in your discipline.
units.fit_note: Also asks instructors to teach AI's limitations, not only its effective use.

units.why: "Give your students sound guidance about AI and how to use it" asks instructors to teach students AI use, which matches P44 (courses teach AI use); the "Digital natives? Not necessarily" remark gives the reason.
units.anchor: Give your students sound guidance about AI and how to use it.

units.why: "Acquiring AI-use skills is a valuable part of a student's education" is a professional-skill rationale for teaching effective AI use (P44), not a rule, so it is informs.
units.anchor: Acquiring AI-use skills is a valuable part of a student’s education.

units.why: "AI can empower your teaching without outsourcing your professional judgment" says what instructors may use AI for and warns against outsourcing judgment: instructor AI use for teaching work (P59), not grading specifically (P46/P101).
units.anchor: can empower your teaching without outsourcing your professional judgment.
units.policy: AI can empower your teaching without outsourcing your professional judgment.

units.why: "keeping your expertise and judgment right at the center" pairs with the line that AI can collaborate with you across your professional life; it permits instructor AI use for workload while keeping the instructor in charge (P59).
units.anchor: extending your capabilities while keeping your expertise and judgment right at the center.
units.policy: AI can collaborate with instructors across their professional life, extending their capabilities while keeping their expertise and judgment right at the center.

units.why: "Use AI for planning complex tasks and communicating more effectively" lists permitted instructor uses of AI for productivity, so P59 (instructor use for teaching work); P76 does not fit because the uses are the instructor's own.
units.anchor: communicating more effectively.
units.policy: Instructors use AI for planning complex tasks and communicating more effectively.
units.fit_note: Productivity and communication uses, not specifically teaching materials or feedback.

units.why: "Enlist AI's assistance with appropriate parts of the research process" permits AI in research with a limit ("appropriate parts"); P62 governs AI in research and scholarship.
units.anchor: appropriate parts
units.policy: Enlist AI's assistance with appropriate parts of the research process.
units.fit_note: Gives no venue, funder or sponsor rules; only says to use AI for appropriate parts.

documents.unit: Ad Hoc Committee on Generative AI in Research and Education (Provost / SVC Research)
documents.title: Considerations for Responsible Use and Recommendations for Generative AI in Research and Education
documents.stance_why: The charge asks for a "positive but careful approach" and notes that GenAI "holds potential to promote equity, improve efficiency, enhance learning". This is conditional welcome, not a ban or a delegation. It sets no course-level rule.
documents.summary: Landing page for the Provost's ad hoc committee report on generative AI in research and education. It gives the committee's charge, method and plan for annual review; the recommendations themselves are in a PDF not saved here.

units.why: The charge to articulate a "positive but careful approach" states the university's overall stance and purpose for GenAI, which is an institution-level framework (P56), permissive with care.
units.anchor: Articulate a “positive but careful approach” to Generative AI

units.why: "constituted and charged by former Provost Cudd, Interim Provost McCarthy, and SVC Rutenbar" says who created the committee and gave it its charge, which is how the guidance was made (P84).
units.anchor: constituted and charged by former Provost Cudd, Interim Provost McCarthy, and SVC Rutenbar

units.why: The committee was charged to "Conduct benchmarking with peer institutions regarding policies or guidance on GenAI uses", benchmarking against peers (P88).
units.anchor: Conduct benchmarking with peer institutions regarding policies or guidance on GenAI uses

units.why: "Map the landscape for uses of GenAI at Pitt (including research and instructional uses)" is a charge to collect evidence on current use; P55 is about effects on learning, so this fits only partly.
units.anchor: Map the landscape for uses of GenAI at Pitt
units.fit_note: Maps where GenAI is used at Pitt; it does not study effects on learning or performance.

units.why: "Crowdsource and gather together GenAI resources, initiatives, activities (e.g., short courses), and programming at Pitt" is a charge to inventory campus AI offerings; no type covers compiling an inventory.
units.anchor: Crowdsource and gather together GenAI resources, initiatives, activities
units.uncovered_note: Charge to compile an inventory of campus GenAI resources, initiatives and programming.

units.why: "Identify key areas in which Pitt can position itself as a leader in the GenAI arena" is an institutional ambition, matching investment in AI capacity and leadership (P122).
units.anchor: Pitt can position itself as a leader in the GenAI arena
units.fit_note: Leadership positioning goal; no funding, infrastructure or research commitment is stated.

units.why: "holds potential to promote equity, improve efficiency, enhance learning, expand knowledge" names benefits of GenAI without making a rule, so P87 (state the benefits).
units.anchor: holds potential to promote equity, improve efficiency, enhance learning

units.why: The committee stresses "the ‘whether’ and ‘if so, how’ questions" that attend use of these tools, asking users to weigh whether AI should be used at all, matching P118.
units.anchor: the ‘whether’ and ‘if so, how’ questions
units.fit_note: Frames the questions as normative to consider, not as a decision procedure for individual users.

units.why: "continue to review the GenAI/AI landscape at least annually" is a review cycle proposed because the technology is rapidly evolving, which is P54.
units.anchor: continue to review the GenAI/AI landscape at least annually for the foreseeable future

units.why: The "Points to Consider" framework "may serve as a ‘living framework’ for future deliberations" sets a framework for AI policy deliberation that is explicitly provisional (P56; P54 covers the review cycle separately).
units.anchor: may serve as a “living framework” for future deliberations
units.frag_start: with its Points to Consider framework,
units.fit_note: Also says the framework is living and will change.

units.why: "The Committee urges that these Points to Consider be employed when implementing its Recommendations" asks implementers to apply the framework when making policy, an institution-level framework rule (P56).
units.anchor: these Points to Consider be employed when implementing its Recommendations

units.why: The "Journal and Publisher Policies Project examining policies regarding use of GenAI in academic publishing" surveys venue rules on AI in scholarship, which is P62.
units.anchor: Journal and Publisher Policies Project examining policies regarding use of GenAI in academic publishing
units.fit_note: Describes a study of publisher policies; no rule for Pitt researchers is stated on this page.

documents.title: Swanson School of Engineering Academic Integrity Policy: Students and Faculty Obligations and Hearing Procedures
documents.stance_why: Violations cover AI help "in a manner not authorized by the instructor" and AI aid "expressly prohibited by the instructor", so AI is barred unless authorized for evaluations, and the instructor decides for other work.
documents.summary: The engineering school's academic integrity policy, covering student obligations, hearing procedures and sanctions. AI appears only in four listed violations, which bar unauthorized AI aid and unacknowledged AI work.

units.why: Item 3 lists receiving help "from another person or artificial intelligence in a manner not authorized by the instructor" during an academic evaluation as a violation, so AI during assessments is barred unless the instructor authorizes it (P22).
units.anchor: Receives assistance during academic evaluation from another person or artificial intelligence in a manner

units.why: Item 8 makes it a violation to depend "on the aid of others or artificial intelligence in a manner expressly prohibited by the instructor" for submitted work, so the instructor sets the rule for AI on assignments (P04); only expressly prohibited use is a violation.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence in a manner expressly prohibited by the instructor
units.fit_note: Also makes expressly prohibited AI aid on submitted work a violation.

units.why: Item 10 forbids presenting "the ideas, representations, or words of another person, persons, or artificial intelligence without customary and proper acknowledgement", so AI use must be acknowledged (P24).
units.anchor: words of another person, persons, or artificial intelligence without customary and proper acknowledgement of sources.
units.frag_start: Presents as one’s own, for academic

units.why: Item 11 forbids submitting "the work of another person or artificial intelligence in a manner which represents the work to be one's own", so AI may not produce work submitted as one's own (P19).
units.anchor: work of another person or artificial intelligence in a manner which represents the work

units.why: The opening says a student "may be found to have violated this obligation" in the listed ways, including the AI items 3, 8, 10 and 11, so unauthorized AI use is handled as an academic integrity violation (P36).
units.anchor: a student may be found to have violated this obligation if, for example, the
units.fit_note: General list of integrity violations; AI appears only in items 3, 8, 10 and 11.

units.why: Faculty must "announce the methods and standards of evaluation" and "the permissible materials or references allowed during evaluation". AI is not named, but this is the duty that tells students what is authorized; P09 is nearest.
units.anchor: in advance of any evaluation, the permissible materials or references allowed
units.fit_note: AI is not named; it is a general duty to announce permissible materials before evaluations.

units.why: The student has "seven (7) days to respond" after being told the instructor believes an integrity offense occurred, a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: the student will be afforded seven (7) days to respond
units.frag_start: the instructor will advise the student
units.fit_note: General integrity procedure; not specific to AI.

units.why: "The faculty, student, and a faculty witness will meet to discuss the allegation" has the instructor talk with the student before escalation, which is P57.
units.anchor: The faculty, student, and a faculty witness will meet to discuss the allegation.
units.fit_note: General integrity procedure, with a faculty witness and an option for a signed written resolution.

units.why: If no resolution is reached, "the instructor will file a written statement of charges" with the Associate Dean, a required reporting step (P81).
units.anchor: the instructor will file a written statement of charges with SSOE’s Associate Dean
units.frag_start: the instructor will file a written

units.why: The student has the right to "be considered innocent until found guilty by clear and convincing evidence", a standard of proof for integrity findings (P69).
units.anchor: considered innocent until found guilty by clear and convincing evidence
units.fit_note: General standard of proof for all integrity cases, not specific to AI.

units.why: The list of student rights ("Present a factual defense through witnesses, personal testimony and other relevant evidence") gives accused students a right to respond, P64.
units.anchor: Present a factual defense through witnesses, personal testimony and other relevant evidence
units.frag_start: vi) Present a factual defense through
units.fit_note: General hearing rights; not specific to AI.

units.why: Listed sanctions include a "letter of reprimand", "Participation in a compulsory academic integrity activity", grade reductions, loss of scholarships, suspension and dismissal, so concrete penalties are stated (P37).
units.anchor: Participation in a compulsory academic integrity activity
units.frag_start: The sanctions which may be imposed
units.frag_end: Dismissal from the University without expectation of readmission.
units.fit_note: General integrity sanctions list; AI is not named.

units.why: "the sanction for a first violation of the Academic Integrity Code will normally be a zero grade for the assignment(s)" plus a reprimand and an online integrity course, a stated first-offense penalty (P37).
units.anchor: will normally be a zero grade for the assignment(s)

units.why: For a fourth offense the penalty is "dismissal from the SSOE program without readmission", an escalating penalty stated in advance (P37); the third-offense suspension is part of the same escalation.
units.anchor: for a fourth offense, dismissal from the SSOE program without readmission to the college

units.why: "within SSOE, the same sanctions will be applied for the same offenses" commits to applying sanctions consistently, matching P124.
units.anchor: within SSOE, the same sanctions will be applied for the same offenses
units.frag_end: the student is a repeat offender.
units.fit_note: Consistency of sanctions among students, not of instructors' AI expectations.

units.why: The Hearing Board "shall be appointed by the Office of the Associate Dean for Academic Affairs", naming who decides integrity cases (P80).
units.anchor: The Academic Integrity Hearing Board shall be appointed by the Office of the Associate Dean
units.fit_note: Names the hearing and appeal bodies for integrity cases; no AI policy owner or exception process.

units.why: Students and faculty may seek review by the Provost or the University Review Board "within five (5) working days", a formal appeal step (P81).
units.anchor: within five (5) working days of the date of the decision letter
units.frag_start: Parties have the right to seek
units.fit_note: General appeal deadline; includes the right to appeal, not only the reporting steps.

notes: The CTL page text is a landing page, so only its tile blurbs were coded; the three syllabus templates mentioned in the collect notes are not in the saved text. The committee report is the landing page only. SSOE units on hearing procedure are general integrity rules that apply to AI misuse; they are coded with fit notes.
